📰 Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde: Trump’s Gaza Plan in One Day

On the same day Trump’s Gaza peace frontman, Nickolay Mladenov, condemned Israel’s national security minister Itamar Ben‑Gvir, he rolled out a glossy “roadmap” for Gaza’s future.

On paper it promises everything: Hamas disarmament through a phased, Palestinian‑led and internationally verified process; expanded humanitarian aid; a technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to run civilian life; new Palestinian security forces; an International Stabilization Force to “reduce friction”; and a gradual IDF withdrawal tied to verified milestones.

It is also a template that has never worked. Variations of “disarm Hamas first, then rebuild, with some kind of neutral forces and rebranded PA security” have been floated after every Gaza round, from “protective edge” language to Trump’s own 20‑point plan, and now reappear under the Board of Peace brand. 

The executor doesn’t exist: there is no Palestinian authority that can both survive in Gaza and be seen as legitimate while doing Israel’s and Washington’s security work for them; there is no real international force that wants to stand between armed factions and an army that answers to no one on the ground.

The euphemisms give it away. “New Palestinian police forces” is a polite way to say “a Palestinian administration that can actually operate in the Strip,” something that has not existed since Hamas took over in 2007. 

“Technocratic council” is a polite way to say “an unelected committee parachuted in by foreign powers,” which no major Palestinian constituency has voted for or endorsed. 

“International stabilization forces” is a polite name for a deployment that no serious state has volunteered to lead, fund, or take casualties for.

Then comes Ben‑Gvir, and the euphemisms evaporate. While Mladenov is selling soft‑focus future governance to the UN and friendly media, Ben‑Gvir posts triumphant clips from the interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla, with activists en route to Gaza shown kneeling on the floor, zip‑tied, mocked under the Israeli anthem and told, effectively, who is master here. 

Even Netanyahu and other Israeli officials felt compelled to distance themselves, but the imagery is brutally clear: a minister of national security performing sovereignty on camera, not as a metaphor, but as bodies on the ground.

Put next to each other, the “roadmap” and the reels are not a contradiction, they are the operating system. Mladenov’s document virtualizes the process: it fixes a respectable, export‑ready version of “the day after” in the public record, so that any future Israeli or US decision can be measured against it, quoted, invoked, defended, or betrayed. 

The fact that there is no executor for most of its clauses matters less than the fact that it exists as a reference point in op‑eds, UN debates, and think‑tank PDFs. In the attention economy, publishing a peace mechanism can be more valuable than having one.

Ben‑Gvir, by contrast, is the unfiltered present tense of the Netanyahu government. No technocrats, no stabilization, no carefully balanced phases — just a minister, detainees, the floor, the handcuffs, and a blunt demonstration of who controls which bodies and which borders. 

If Mladenov is Dr. Jekyll, manufacturing a civilized horizon for Gaza under Trump’s Board of Peace brand, Ben‑Gvir is Mr. Hyde, acting out the raw priorities of the current Israeli leadership in real time.

The success of the whole construction does not depend on implementation on the ground. It depends on whether Trump can keep the Jekyll story loud enough in Washington and abroad to offset the Hyde footage coming from Israel — long enough to call the project a “historic step toward peace,” even if Gaza never sees the version laid out on paper.

The real explosives are not in the language of the text but in what it glides over: Iran’s enriched uranium and control of the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran does not want to surrender its nuclear leverage. Washington does not want to admit it can no longer dictate the rules of every oil route on earth.

Tehran gets a narrative that it cracked the sanctions wall and dragged the US into negotiations “on equal footing.” Pakistan gets to pose as the new indispensable mediator of the Greater Middle East, a budget Switzerland with nukes and economic collapse.

Trump’s Visit to Beijing Apparently Turned Into One of His Biggest Political Setbacks


China and Russia condemned U.S. President Donald Trump's Golden Dome missile defence shield plans and Washington's "irresponsible" nuclear policy at a summit on Wednesday, a week after President ​Xi Jinping hosted Trump in Beijing.

A joint statement issued after Xi's summit with Putin served to underline that, while the Chinese leader seeks stable and constructive relations with ‌Trump, he differs fundamentally with him on key issues where China's position is closely aligned with Russia's.

The treaty lapsed in February and Trump did not respond to Moscow's proposal to extend its missile and warhead limits by a year - something that some U.S. politicians argued would have hindered the U.S. from responding to a nuclear build-up by China.

Yet while ​speaking in unison on global security issues, the two leaders failed to reach a breakthrough that Moscow has long been seeking, a contract for a new pipeline that would enable it to more than ​double the amount of natural gas it sells to China.

Xi was wrapping up a remarkable week of diplomacy in which he met the leaders of China's ⁠most powerful strategic rival and one of its closest partners.

With Trump seeking an exit from a war with Iran and Putin's forces largely bogged down in Ukraine, the summits provided China's leader with a chance to showcase Beijing ​as a pillar of global stability and an indispensable diplomatic player.

"Xi does appear to hold the stronger position relative to both Putin and Trump. Both leaders are grappling with conflicts of their own making that have proven far more ​difficult to resolve than initially anticipated," 
said Patricia Kim, a foreign policy fellow at the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

"Xi, meanwhile, has been able to focus more squarely on strengthening China internally while projecting an image of a stable and confident great power on the global stage."

While the summit with Trump was largely about managing tensions, the encounter with Putin posed a different challenge - how to demonstrate progress in a relationship that the two sides have already proclaimed is "without limits".

Xi and Putin, who have met more than 40 times, both ​stressed the closeness of the Russia-China ties that they sealed in 2022 with the signing of a strategic partnership treaty, less than three weeks before Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

During Putin's last visit in September 2025, Russian gas giant Gazprom said both sides had agreed to move forward with Power of Siberia 2, a prospective 2,600 km (1,616-mile) pipeline to carry 50 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas per year from Russia to China via Mongolia.

Xi said on Wednesday that cooperation in energy and resource connectivity should be the "ballast stone" in China-Russia relations, mentioning the pipeline.

Key issues such as gas pricing remain unresolved, and analysts expect negotiations could take years.

The Kremlin said both sides had reached a "fundamental understanding on the parameters" of the project, although no details or clear timeline were agreed. 

Xi welcomed Putin with ​an honour guard and a gun salute at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, as children waved Chinese and Russian flags. 

They later dined on ​Peking duck and Jinhua cured ⁠ham at a banquet, and drank tea together with a small number of close aides, before Putin's plane departed.
Xi said the countries should focus on long-term strategy and promote a "more just and reasonable" global governance system, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
In their joint declaration, the two sides outlined ⁠plans for further ​cooperation across a vast range of areas, from artificial intelligence to protecting rare tigers, leopards and pandas.

They accused the United States and Israel ​of violating international law by attacking Iran, and expressed their "resolute opposition to hegemonism and unilateralism".

📈 In 2025, cryptocurrency fraud losses exceeded $11 billion, with investment schemes accounting for the largest share at over $7 billion. The FBI reported that the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) received more than 181,000 complaints, a 20% increase from the previous year. The average loss per victim was approximately $62,600, with thousands losing over $100,000.

🔔 The most affected group was individuals aged 60 and above, who suffered losses of around $4.4 billion. This was followed by the 50-59 age group with losses of about $2.1 billion, and the 40-49 age group with over $1.5 billion. The report highlighted that fraudsters often employ complex social engineering tactics targeting older adults.

📊 Fraud losses have been steadily increasing over the years, reaching a peak in 2025. In 2018, losses were only in the tens of millions of dollars, but by 2025, they had surged to over $11 billion. The states with the highest number of complaints were California, Texas, and Florida.

🤖 The report also noted a rise in AI-related crimes, with over 8,700 cases and approximately $740 million in losses.
